title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal, Randomized Controlled Trial
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI-powered mobile app can proactively improve young adults’ well-being, rather than waiting to treat mental health problems after they emerge. The authors frame the work as a strengths-based alternative to deficit-oriented mental health tools, aiming to boost positive affect, resilience, belonging, mindfulness, and flourishing while buffering against declines in well-being.

The intervention was the Flourish app, an iOS/Android mobile application featuring an AI chatbot (“Sunnie”), brief check-ins, personalized recommendations for science-based well-being activities, and weekly summaries. The system used large language models to adapt its tone, content, and suggestions in real time, and included safety and escalation protocols for high-risk language. The study ran for six weeks in Fall 2024 across three U.S. institutions: Chapman University, the University of Washington, and Foothill College.

A total of 486 undergraduate students were randomly assigned to app access or a waitlist control. Outcomes were measured with repeated self-report surveys across four waves. The treatment group showed significant improvements in positive affect, calm, social well-being indicators such as loneliness and belonging, and overall well-being measures including resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing. Effects on negative affect, depression, anxiety, stress, and academic self-efficacy were not significant. The authors conclude that a purpose-built generative AI system can deliver scalable, preventive well-being support, though future studies should test active controls and longer-term effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered, multi-site randomized controlled trial with longitudinal follow-up and validated measures, which is strong causal evidence. Some concerns remain because the control was waitlist rather than active, and engagement/back-end usage data were self-reported rather than directly logged.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are statistically significant but modest in magnitude (e.g., positive affect d≈0.23 to 0.33; beta values around 0.03-0.05). The intervention shows promise for a college mental health population, but the impacts are small and focused on well-being rather than academic or clinical outcomes.

interventions.use_case: generative AI-powered mobile well-being app delivering brief check-ins, chatbot conversations, and science-based micro-activities with personalized recommendations and weekly insights

finding.finding_summary: In a 6-week multi-institutional RCT (n=486 undergraduates), access to the Flourish app improved several well-being indicators versus waitlist control. The strongest effects were on positive affect (Condition × Time b=0.22, p=.020; Week 6 d=0.33), resilience (b=0.11, p=.047), mindfulness (b=0.19, p=.045), and flourishing (b=0.19, p=.032), while negative affect showed no effect.
finding.measure: Positive affect, negative affect, resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing scales
finding.effect_size: reported as d=0.23 at Week 4 and d=0.33 at Week 6 for positive affect; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also improved social well-being in the same RCT (n=486). Loneliness decreased more steeply in the treatment group than control (b=-0.05, p=.038), and belonging improved (b=0.06, p=.030), with a marginal increase in closeness to the university (b=0.04, p=.070).
finding.measure: UCLA 3-item loneliness, campus belonging, and closeness-to-school measures
